Layer 1 The United States has listed 50 countries whose citizens must pay a visa bond of up to $20,000 when applying for certain visitor visas, including Nigeria, according to the US Department of State.
The measure applies to eligible applicants for B-1 business and B-2 tourist visas travelling on passports issued by the listed countries. The bond amounts are $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000, with the specific amount determined by a consular officer during the visa interview.
In a notice published on October 2, 2026, the Department of State outlined the countries subject to the visa bond programme and their respective implementation dates.
The programme operates under Section 221(g)(3) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, with the department stating that the requirement applies regardless of where an applicant submits their visa application.

Nigerian citizens applying for B-1 business or B-2 tourist visas may be required to post a bond of $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000 if they are otherwise eligible for the visa.
The amount is determined during the visa interview. The bond is an additional financial requirement and does not guarantee that the applicant will receive a visa.
Applicants must submit Department of Homeland Security Form I-352 and agree to the bond’s terms through the US Department of the Treasury’s Pay.gov platform.
The department warns applicants not to pay a bond before being instructed to do so by a consular officer. Applicants are expected to use the specific payment link supplied through official instructions.
The bond may be paid by the applicant or a third party, such as a relative, friend or business associate. However, the name of the person identified as the bond obligor on Form I-352 must match the name of the person making the payment.
If the bond conditions are satisfied, the money is refundable under the programme’s terms.
The programme also imposes travel conditions on people who post visa bonds.
According to the State Department, bond holders must enter and leave the United States through designated commercial air ports of entry, including US Customs and Border Protection preclearance locations.
They are not permitted to use charter aircraft, general aviation, land borders or sea ports of entry under the stated bond conditions.
Failure to comply with the designated entry and exit requirements could result in problems with entry or the recording of a traveller’s departure.
The department outlined several circumstances under which a bond may be cancelled and the deposit returned automatically.
